paragraphs: The Embassy to Achilles.

The Trojans kept watch. But Panic, the comrade of blood-stained Rout, had taken a firm hold on the Achaeans, and all their princes were in despair. Two winds blow from Thrace, the north wind and the northwest wind, and they can spring up suddenly and stir the sea to fury. At once the dark waves lift their heads and scatter seaweed in every direction. The hearts of the Achaeans were churned up in just that way.

In dismay, the son of Atreus told the heralds to call the people to a council one by one, but not to shout the news aloud. He hurried to call them himself as well, and they sat in the assembly, sick at heart. Agamemnon wept like a running stream or a waterfall down the side of a sheer cliff. With many heavy sighs he spoke to the Achaeans. “My friends,” he said, “princes and councilors of the Argives, heaven has laid a heavy hand on me. Cruel Zeus solemnly promised me that I would sack the city of Troy before I went home. He has cheated me. Now he orders me to go back to Argos with no glory, after losing so many of my people. This is the will of Zeus, who has brought down many proud cities and will bring down others, for his power is above all. So now let us all do as I say. Let us sail back to our own country, for we will not take Troy.”

So he spoke, and the sons of the Achaeans sat sorrowful for a long while, and all of them kept silent. At last Diomedes of the loud battle cry answered. “Son of Atreus, I will rebuke your folly, as is my right in council. Do not be angry that I do. First, you attacked me in front of all the Danaans and called me a coward and no soldier. The Argives, young and old, know that you did. But the son of scheming Cronus gave you only half his gifts. He gave you honor as our chief ruler, but he did not give you valor, which is the highest of both right and might. Sir, do you really think the sons of the Achaeans are as unwarlike and cowardly as you say they are? If your own mind is set on going home, then go. The way is open to you. The many ships that followed you from Mycene stand lined up on the seashore. But the rest of us will stay here until we have sacked Troy. And even if these men too turn homeward with their ships, Sthenelus and I will go on fighting until we reach the goal of Ilium, for heaven was with us when we came.”

The sons of the Achaeans shouted their approval of what Diomedes had said, and soon Nestor rose to speak. “Son of Tydeus,” he said, “your prowess in war is beyond question, and in council you excel all men of your own age. None of the Achaeans can brush aside what you say or argue against it. But you have not yet reached the end of the matter. You are young. You could be the youngest of my own children. Still, you have spoken wisely, and you have advised the chief of the Achaeans with good judgment. Even so, I am older than you, and I will tell you everything. So let no man, not even King Agamemnon, ignore what I say, for whoever stirs up civil strife is a clanless, hearthless outlaw.

“Now, though, let us obey the commands of night and get our suppers. Let the sentinels, every one of them, camp by the trench outside the wall. These are my instructions to the young men. When they have been seen to, son of Atreus, you give your orders, for you are the most royal of us all. Prepare a feast for your councilors. It is right and reasonable that you should. There is plenty of wine in your tents, which the ships of the Achaeans bring from Thrace every day. You have everything you need to entertain guests, and you have many subjects. When many are gathered, you can follow the man whose counsel is wisest. And we badly need shrewd and prudent counsel, for the enemy has lit his watchfires close to our ships. Who can help being dismayed? This night will either ruin our army or save it.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said. The sentinels went out in their armor under Nestor’s son Thrasymedes, a captain of the host, and the bold warriors Ascalaphus and Ialmenus. With them were Meriones, Aphareus and Deipyrus, and the son of Creion, noble Lycomedes. There were seven captains of the sentinels, and a hundred youths armed with long spears went with each of them. They took their places midway between the trench and the wall. Then they lit their fires, and every man got his supper.

The son of Atreus then invited many councilors of the Achaeans to his quarters and prepared a great feast in their honor. They helped themselves to the good things set before them. When they had had enough to eat and drink, old Nestor, whose counsel was always truest, was the first to lay his thoughts before them. He addressed them sincerely and with goodwill, in these words.

“Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, with you I will both begin my speech and end it, for you are king over many people. Zeus has also granted you the scepter and the duty to uphold justice, so that you may look after the people under you. That is why you, above all others, must both speak and listen, and act on the advice of anyone else who chooses to speak wisely. Everything depends on you and your commands, so I will say what I think is best. No man will have a truer mind than mine has been since the hour when you, sir, angered Achilles by taking the girl Briseis from his tent, against my judgment. I urged you not to do it. But you gave in to your own pride and dishonored a hero whom heaven itself had honored, for you still hold the prize that was awarded to him. Now let us think how we can appease him, with presents and with fair words that will win him over.”

And King Agamemnon answered, “Sir, you have rightly rebuked my folly. I was wrong. I admit it. A man whom heaven befriends is an army in himself, and Zeus has shown that he befriends this man by destroying so many of the Achaeans. I was blinded by passion and gave in to my worse mind. So I will make amends and give him great gifts as atonement. I will name them in front of you all. I will give him seven tripods that have never yet been on the fire, and ten talents of gold. I will give him twenty iron cauldrons and twelve strong horses that have won races and carried off prizes. A man is rich indeed in land and gold if he has as many prizes as my horses have won me. I will give him seven excellent workwomen, Lesbians, whom I chose for myself when he took Lesbos, all of surpassing beauty. I will give him these, and with them the one I took from him earlier, the daughter of Briseus. And I swear a great oath that I never went up into her bed, and never lay with her as men and women do.

“All this I will give him now. And if later the gods grant that I sack the city of Priam, let him come when we Achaeans are dividing the spoil and load his ship with as much gold and bronze as he likes. Let him also take twenty Trojan women, the loveliest after Helen herself. Then, when we reach Achaean Argos, wealthiest of all lands, he will be my son-in-law. I will show him the same honor as my own dear son Orestes, who is being raised in all abundance. I have three daughters, Chrysothemis, Laodice, and Iphianassa. Let him take whichever he chooses to the house of Peleus, freely and without wedding gifts. I will add a dowry besides, such as no man ever gave his daughter. I will give him seven well-established cities: Cardamyle, Enope, and Hire, where there is grass; holy Pherae and the rich meadows of Anthea; Aepea too, and the vine-clad slopes of Pedasus. All of them are near the sea, on the borders of sandy Pylos. The men who live there are rich in cattle and sheep. They will honor him with gifts as though he were a god, and obey his mild decrees. All this I will do if he gives up his anger now. Let him yield. Only Hades is utterly ruthless and unyielding, and that is why he is the god most hated by mankind. Besides, I am older and more royal than he is. So let him obey me now.”

Then Nestor answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men: the gifts you offer are not small ones. Let us send chosen messengers to the tent of Achilles son of Peleus without delay. Let those go whom I name. Let Phoenix, dear to Zeus, lead the way. Let Ajax and Odysseus follow, and let the heralds Odius and Eurybates go with them. Now bring water for our hands, and tell everyone to keep silent while we pray to Zeus the son of Cronus, in case he will have mercy on us.”

So he spoke, and his words pleased them well. Servants poured water over the guests’ hands, and pages filled the mixing bowls with wine and water and handed it around, giving every man his drink offering. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as each wanted, the envoys set out from the tent of Agamemnon son of Atreus. Nestor looked first at one and then at another, but most especially at Odysseus, and urged them hard to win over the noble son of Peleus.

They went along the shore of the sounding sea and prayed earnestly to earth-encircling Poseidon that the proud spirit of the son of Aeacus would be favorable to them. They reached the ships and tents of the Myrmidons and found Achilles playing a lyre, a beautiful one of skilled workmanship, with a silver cross-bar. It was part of the spoils he had taken when he sacked the city of Eetion. He was entertaining himself with it and singing the deeds of heroes. He was alone with Patroclus, who sat opposite him in silence, waiting for him to stop singing. Odysseus and Ajax now came in, with Odysseus leading the way, and stood before him. Achilles sprang from his seat with the lyre still in his hand, and Patroclus rose too when he saw the strangers. Achilles greeted them. “Welcome, all hail. You must have come on some great matter, you who are still dearest to me of the Achaeans, for all my anger.”

With this he led them forward and had them sit on seats covered with purple rugs. Then he spoke to Patroclus, who was close by him. “Son of Menoetius, set a larger bowl on the table, mix less water with the wine, and give every man his cup. These are very dear friends, and they are under my roof now.”

Patroclus did as his comrade told him. He set the chopping block in front of the fire and laid on it the loin of a sheep, the loin of a goat, and the chine of a fat hog. Automedon held the meat while Achilles chopped it. Then Achilles sliced the pieces and put them on spits, while the son of Menoetius made the fire burn high. When the flame had died down, Patroclus spread out the embers, laid the spits over them, lifted them and set them on the spit racks, and sprinkled them with salt. When the meat was roasted, he put it on platters and passed bread around the table in fair baskets, while Achilles dealt out the portions. Then Achilles took his seat facing Odysseus, against the opposite wall, and told his comrade Patroclus to offer sacrifice to the gods. Patroclus cast the offerings into the fire, and they helped themselves to the good things set before them. When they had had enough to eat and drink, Ajax made a sign to Phoenix. Odysseus saw it, filled his cup with wine, and drank to Achilles.

“Hail, Achilles,” he said. “We have had no lack of good cheer, either in the tent of Agamemnon or here. There has been plenty to eat and drink, but our thoughts are not on such things. Sir, we face great disaster, and without your help we do not know whether we will save our fleet or lose it. The Trojans and their allies have camped close to our ships and the wall. They have lit watchfires throughout their host and think nothing can now stop them from falling on our fleet. Zeus has also sent lightning on their right. Hector, in all his glory, rages like a maniac. Confident that Zeus is with him, he fears neither god nor man. He has gone raving mad and prays for the day to come. He vows to hew the high sterns of our ships to pieces, set fire to their hulls, and slaughter the Achaeans while they are dazed and choked with smoke. I fear greatly that heaven will make his boasting good, and that it will be our lot to die at Troy, far from our home in Argos. Up, then, and late though it is, save the sons of the Achaeans, who are failing before the fury of the Trojans. You will bitterly regret it later if you do not, for once the harm is done there will be no curing it. Think before it is too late, and save the Danaans from destruction.

“My good friend, when your father Peleus sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, did he not give you this charge? ‘My son, Athena and Hera will make you strong if they choose, but keep your high temper in check, for goodwill is the better course. Avoid pointless quarrels, and the Achaeans, old and young, will respect you more for it.’ Those were his words, but you have forgotten them. Even now, though, calm down and put your anger aside. Agamemnon will make you great amends if you forgive him. Listen, and I will tell you what he said in his tent that he will give you. He will give you seven tripods that have never yet been on the fire, and ten talents of gold; twenty iron cauldrons, and twelve strong horses that have won races and carried off prizes. A man is rich indeed in land and gold if he has as many prizes as these horses have won for Agamemnon. He will also give you seven excellent workwomen, Lesbians, whom he chose for himself when you took Lesbos, all of surpassing beauty. He will give you these, and with them the one he took from you earlier, the daughter of Briseus, and he will swear a great oath that he never went up into her bed and never lay with her as men and women do. He will give you all this right now. And if later the gods grant that he sack the city of Priam, you can come when we Achaeans are dividing the spoil and load your ship with as much gold and bronze as you like. You can take twenty Trojan women, the loveliest after Helen herself. Then, when we reach Achaean Argos, wealthiest of all lands, you will be his son-in-law, and he will show you the same honor as his own dear son Orestes, who is being raised in all abundance. Agamemnon has three daughters, Chrysothemis, Laodice, and Iphianassa. You may take whichever you choose to the house of Peleus, freely and without wedding gifts. He will add a dowry besides, such as no man ever gave his daughter, and will give you seven well-established cities: Cardamyle, Enope, and Hire, where there is grass; holy Pherae and the rich meadows of Anthea; Aepea too, and the vine-clad slopes of Pedasus. All of them are near the sea, on the borders of sandy Pylos. The men who live there are rich in cattle and sheep. They will honor you with gifts as though you were a god, and obey your mild decrees. All this he will do if you give up your anger now. And even if you hate both him and his gifts with all your heart, still pity the rest of the Achaeans, who are being worn down throughout their host. They will honor you as a god, and you will win great glory from them. You might even kill Hector. He will come within your reach, for he is infatuated, and he declares that not one Danaan the ships have brought can stand against him.”

Achilles answered, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, I must tell you plainly, and with a fixed purpose, that I want no more of this cajoling, from whatever quarter it comes. I hate like the gates of hell the man who says one thing while hiding another in his heart. So I will say what I mean. Neither Agamemnon son of Atreus nor any other of the Danaans will appease me, for I see that I get no thanks for all my fighting. The man who fights fares no better than the man who does not. Coward and hero are held in equal honor, and death deals the same measure to the man who works and the man who is idle. I have gained nothing from all my hardships, with my life always in my hand. A bird, when she has found a morsel, takes it to her nestlings and goes hungry herself. In the same way I have lain awake many a long night, and fought many a bloody battle by day against men who were fighting for their women. With my ships I have taken twelve cities, and eleven more around Troy I have stormed with my men by land. From every one of them I took great store of wealth, and I gave all of it up to Agamemnon son of Atreus. He stayed where he was by his ships, and of what came to him he gave out little and kept much himself.

“Still, he did hand out some prizes of honor among the chieftains and kings, and they have them yet. From me alone of the Achaeans he took the woman I delighted in. Let him keep her and sleep with her. Why, tell me, must the Argives fight the Trojans? What made the son of Atreus gather the host and bring them? Was it not for the sake of Helen? Are the sons of Atreus the only men in the world who love their wives? Any man of common decent feeling loves and cherishes his own woman, as I loved this one with my whole heart, though she was only the fruit of my spear. Agamemnon has taken her from me. He has cheated me. I know him. Let him tempt me no further, for he will not move me. Let him look to you, Odysseus, and the other princes, to save his ships from burning. He has done much without me already. He has built a wall. He has dug a trench, deep and wide, all around it, and planted stakes inside it. But even so he cannot stop the murderous might of Hector. As long as I fought among the Achaeans, Hector did not let the battle range far from the city walls. He would come as far as the Scaean gates and the oak tree, and no further. Once he stood to meet me, and he barely escaped my onslaught. Now, since I am in no mood to fight him, I will offer sacrifice to Zeus and all the gods tomorrow. I will draw my ships into the water and stock them properly. Tomorrow morning, if you care to look, you will see my ships on the Hellespont and my men rowing out to sea with all their might. If great Poseidon grants me a fair passage, in three days I will be in Phthia. I have much there that I left behind when I came here to my sorrow. I will bring back still more gold, red copper, fair women, and iron, my share of the spoils we have taken. But one prize, the man who gave it has insolently taken away. Tell him all this as I now tell you, and tell him in public, so that the Achaeans may hate him and beware of him, in case he thinks he can still dupe others, for his effrontery never fails him.
